title: Senior's toolkit: testing failure on purpose
summary: Time a call, read error headers, send idempotency keys and trace ids, inject latency and load: prove your timeouts and retries work.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: testing failure on purpose
steps.body: Timeouts, retries and breakers that were never exercised do not work. These commands let you make failures happen and watch what your integration does.

toolkit.what: Puts a hard limit on a call, the way your client should. Combined with `-w` it shows where the time went.
flags: give up if the TCP/TLS connection takes over 2 s
give up if the whole call takes over 5 s (exit code 28)

toolkit.what: Dumps the response headers to the screen and the body to a file, so you can read `Retry-After`, `Content-Type: application/problem+json` and the error body together.
flags: write the response headers to stdout

toolkit.what: Retries transient failures (timeouts, 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504) with a growing delay, and honours `Retry-After`. The shell equivalent of a retry policy.
flags: stop retrying after 20 s in total
also retry other errors (use with care)
toolkit.when: scripts and health checks that must survive a restart

toolkit.what: Sends the same key twice to prove a retried POST does not create a second order. The server should return the first result again.
flags: a unique id per logical operation, reused on every retry
toolkit.example: key=$(uuidgen); for i in 1 2; do curl -sS --json @order.json -H "Idempotency-Key: $key" http://localhost:8080/orders; done

toolkit.what: Sends a W3C trace context header with a trace id you choose, so you can find that one request in the logs of every service it touched.
flags: 00-<32 hex trace id>-<16 hex parent id>-01
version, trace id, parent span id, flags (`01` = sampled)
toolkit.when: debugging one request across gateway, routes and backends

toolkit.what: Toxiproxy sits between your service and a dependency and injects latency, timeouts or dropped connections on command.
flags: hold the connection and never answer
toolkit.example: toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=3000 payments
toolkit.when: proving that your timeout fires and the breaker opens

toolkit.what: A load test written in JavaScript. Run it while a dependency is slowed to see whether threads pile up or the breaker sheds load.
flags: fail the run when, say, p95 latency goes over 500 ms

steps.prompt: Match each header or option to its job.
pairs: make a retried POST safe to repeat
follow one request through every service
the server says how long to wait before trying again
give up on the whole call after 5 seconds

steps.prompt: Under load, the orders API stops answering at all, even `/health`. Payments (one of its dependencies) became slow at the same time. Orders calls payments with `HttpClient` and no timeout set beyond the default. What is the likely cause?
options: Requests wait up to 100 s each on payments (HttpClient's default timeout), so every worker is busy waiting and nothing else is served
The health endpoint has a bug
The database ran out of connections because of retries
steps.explain: A slow dependency is worse than a dead one: without a short timeout every request holds resources while it waits. Set a timeout well under your own budget, add a breaker, and prove it with `toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency` plus a k6 run.

steps.prompt: Prove a retried POST creates one order: send it twice with the same key.
steps.explain: Both calls must carry the same key. A fresh key on the retry, or a per-request id like `X-Request-Id`, would let the server create two orders.
W3C trace context is `version-traceid-parentid-flags`: `00`, 32 hex digits, 16 hex digits, and `01` for sampled. OpenTelemetry and most gateways read and forward it.

steps.prompt: Order a failure test of the payments timeout.
lines: Start a k6 run against orders: k6 run --vus 50 --duration 2m load-orders.js
Slow payments down: toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=3000 payments
Watch orders' p95 latency and error rate: requests should fail fast, not hang
Remove the toxic: toxiproxy-cli toxic remove -n latency_downstream payments
Check that orders recovers on its own once payments is fast again
also: Slow payments down: toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=3000 payments
Start a k6 run against orders: k6 run --vus 50 --duration 2m load-orders.js
Watch orders' p95 latency and error rate: requests should fail fast, not hang
Remove the toxic: toxiproxy-cli toxic remove -n latency_downstream payments
Check that orders recovers on its own once payments is fast again
steps.explain: Starting the load first gives you a healthy baseline to compare with; slowing payments first works too. What matters is that the load runs while the toxic is in place, and that you check recovery after removing it.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Every time you add a timeout, a retry or a breaker, break the dependency on purpose and watch what happens. Send a `traceparent` you chose when you debug, so one search finds the request in every log.
